plan: In a second-price auction (winner pays second-highest bid), bidding one's true value is a weakly dominant strategy regardless of what other bidders do. This holds true even against strategic, rational opponents—my optimal bid doesn't depend on their beliefs about me, since truthful bidding maximizes expected profit in all cases. With my value at $9, I should bid exactly $9 to ensure I only win when profitable and pay a fair price if I do win.

In a second-price auction, bidding your true value is the dominant strategy regardless of what others do, since you pay the second-highest bid, not your own. Bidding higher than my value risks winning and paying more than the item is worth to me; bidding lower reduces my chance of winning profitable situations. With a value of $9, truthful bidding maximizes expected profit given the mechanism's incentive structure.

In a second-price sealed-bid auction, bidding your true value is a weakly dominant strategy regardless of what other bidders do. This holds because you pay the second-highest bid, not your own bid, so overbidding risks paying more than the item is worth, while underbidding risks losing profitable opportunities. Since other bidders are rational and will also bid truthfully (or close to it), the best response is to bid exactly my value of $34, ensuring optimal expected profit.
